lead: Paul, on his way to Jerusalem, calls the elders of Ephesus to Miletus and speaks to them as a father who knows he will not see his children again. He wants only to finish his course and the ministry received from the Lord Jesus. In the Gospel Jesus lifts his eyes to heaven and begins his great prayer: “Father, the hour has come; glorify your Son.” Both readings are farewells, and both look to a work completed. Psalm 68 blesses the Lord who daily bears us up.

set: Paul is hurrying to reach Jerusalem by Pentecost (20:16). He does not go up to Ephesus but sends for its elders to come to him at Miletus, a port some distance to the south. This is the only speech in Acts that Paul gives to Christians, to the leaders of a church he founded. It is a farewell speech, like the farewells of Jacob, Moses, Joshua and Samuel, and like Jesus’ own farewell at the Last Supper.
Background. Paul had spent about three years at Ephesus (20:31). It was there, many scholars think, that he wrote 1 Corinthians (1 Corinthians 16:8).
str: vv. 17–18a: the elders of Ephesus come to Miletus.
vv. 18b–21: looking back: humility, tears, trials, teaching in public and from house to house.
vv. 22–24: looking ahead: bound by the Spirit for Jerusalem, prison and persecution awaiting.
vv. 25–27: they will not see him again; he has declared the whole purpose of God.
kw: The leaders of the local church. In v. 28 (tomorrow’s reading) Paul calls the same men episkopoi, overseers. In this early period the two names were used for the same ministry; later the bishop (episkopos) came to be distinguished from the presbyters.
Paul pictures his life as a race to be finished. 2 Timothy 4:7 uses the same word: “I have finished the race”.
“The whole purpose of God” (v. 27): God’s saving plan, all of it. Paul did not choose only the easy or popular parts of the Gospel.
vv: serving the Lord with all humility and with tears,
The word for “serving” is the work of a slave. Paul’s ministry was not a career but service, and his tears show how much the people mattered to him.
teaching you publicly and from house to house,
The early Church gathered in homes. Teaching the faith in the family and the home is as old as the Church.
And now, as a captive to the Spirit, I am on my way to Jerusalem, not knowing what will happen to me there,
Literally “bound in the Spirit”. Before he is bound with chains in Jerusalem (21:33), he is already bound by the Spirit. He goes as Jesus went up to Jerusalem, knowing that suffering waits.
But I do not count my life of any value to myself, if only I may finish my course and the ministry that I received from the Lord Jesus,
Paul does not despise his life; he holds it as less than the mission. The ministry is not his own: he “received” it.
ch: The Church reads this speech as a mirror for every bishop and priest, and for all who serve in the Church. Commentators often call the Miletus speech Paul’s pastoral testament. Paul’s words “the whole purpose of God” remind teachers of the faith to hand on the whole Gospel, the hard parts with the consoling ones. The Second Vatican Council asks priests to be fathers and shepherds to their people, giving their lives as Christ did (Presbyterorum Ordinis 6 and 13, in substance).

set: John 17 is the longest prayer of Jesus in the Gospels, spoken at the end of the Last Supper before he goes out to the garden. It is often called the “priestly prayer”: Jesus, about to offer himself, prays for himself (vv. 1–5), for his disciples (vv. 6–19), and for all who will believe through their word (vv. 20–26). Today and tomorrow we hear the first two parts.
str: vv. 1–3: glorify your Son; eternal life is to know you.
vv. 4–5: the work finished; the glory before the world existed.
vv. 6–8: the disciples received the word and believed.
vv. 9–11a: I pray for them; they are in the world, I am coming to you.
kw: In John, the Son is glorified on the Cross, where God’s love is shown in full. The “hour” of glory is the hour of the Passion.
Not only life after death but the life of God begun now. Verse 3 defines it: to know the Father and Jesus Christ whom he sent.
To know in the biblical sense is not only to have information but to be in a living relationship. Eternal life is friendship with God.
vv: he looked up to heaven and said, “Father, the hour has come; glorify your Son so that the Son may glorify you,
Jesus looks up to heaven as he did at the tomb of Lazarus (11:41). The priest at Mass, in the First Eucharistic Prayer, recalls that at the Last Supper Jesus raised his eyes to heaven.
And this is eternal life, that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent.
The faith of Israel in the one God, “the only true God”, is kept whole. Jesus Christ is named with him because the Father is known in the Son whom he sent.
I glorified you on earth by finishing the work that you gave me to do.
He speaks as if the Cross were already done. On the Cross he will say, “It is finished” (19:30), with a verb from the same root.
I am asking on their behalf; I am not asking on behalf of the world,

This does not mean Jesus does not care for the world, which the Father so loved (3:16). Here he prays for the disciples whom he is sending into the world, so that through them the world may believe (17:21).
ch: The Catechism devotes a section to this prayer and says that Christian tradition rightly calls it the “priestly” prayer of Jesus, the prayer of the high priest at the hour of his Passover (CCC 2746–2747). St Cyril of Alexandria, commenting on this chapter, saw Christ here as our high priest and intercessor (in substance). Jesus prays now as he will pray for ever at the Father’s right hand: “he always lives to make intercession” (Hebrews 7:25).

qa: What does Jesus mean by “the glory that I had in your presence before the world existed”?

These words (17:5) show that the Son existed with the Father before creation, as the Prologue says: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God” (1:1). The eternal Son became man; in his Passion and Resurrection his humanity enters the glory that he always had as God.
study: Paul says he wants only to finish his course. What is the course God has given me, and what is distracting me from it?
Jesus says eternal life is to know the Father and the Son. What helps me to know God, not only to know about him?
